tldr: Claude chooses a tool by reading its **name and description** — the docs call detailed descriptions “by far the most important factor in tool performance”. Say **what the tool does, when to use it and when not to (name the alternative), what each parameter means, what it returns and doesn't**, with input formats and edge cases. Tools whose descriptions **overlap** get confused; **generic** tools should be **split** into purpose-specific ones with clear input/output contracts; and a **keyword rule in the system prompt** can silently override all of it.
mentalModel: Tool descriptions are job adverts for a team the model is staffing: vague adverts (“does stuff with documents”) get the wrong hire, two identical adverts are a coin toss, and a manager's note saying “anyone who says ‘document’ goes to Sam” overrides every advert.
whatItIs:
A tool definition is `name` + `description` + `input_schema` (+ optional `input_examples`). The API builds a special system prompt from
your tool definitions and your own system prompt, and the model decides from that which tool (if any) to call (docs: define tools).
The exam guide's TS 2.1 (Guide §6, p.9) is about writing those definitions so the model routes correctly. The round trip around a call —
`stop_reason: "tool_use"` → run → `tool_result` → continue — is TS 1.1, taught on D1.1.

**Sub-concepts — each with its picture to remember**

| # | Sub-concept | 🧭 Mental model | ⭐ Exam reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Description = the selection signal | A job advert: the model hires from the advert, not from the code behind it. | ⭐ TS 2.1 · Knowledge 1 · p.9 |
| 2 | Formats, examples, edge cases, boundaries | A form with a filled-in sample: “ORD-1001, not 1001”; “email only? use the other desk”. | ⭐ TS 2.1 · Knowledge 2 · p.9 |
| 3 | Overlap → misrouting | Two shop signs saying the same thing: customers walk into whichever comes first. | ⭐ TS 2.1 · Knowledge 3 · p.9 |
| 4 | Keyword rules in the system prompt | A sticky note “anyone who says X goes to Y” overrides every sign in the building. | ⭐ TS 2.1 · Knowledge 4, Skill 4 · p.9 |
| 5 | Differentiate & rename | Name the job, not the verb: extract_web_results says what goes in. | ⭐ TS 2.1 · Skills 1–2 · p.9 |
| 6 | Split generic tools | One “handyman” advert vs three specialists with a clear brief each. | ⭐ TS 2.1 · Skill 3 · p.9 |
| 7 | input_examples, namespacing, consolidation | Samples on the form; a department prefix on every desk; one desk per closely related task. | 📘 docs (define tools § Best practices) |

**Anatomy of a good description** (docs checklist)

| # | Say… | Example (lookup_order) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | What it does | Looks up one order's status, amount and delivery date by its order id |
| 2 | When to use it | The user gives an order id |
| 3 | When NOT to use it — and what instead | Only an email? Use get_customer first |
| 4 | What each parameter means / looks like | order_id is ORD-#### (e.g. ORD-1001); prefix a bare number |
| 5 | What it returns — and doesn't | Status and amount; not customer details |

**Split or consolidate?** The guide splits a *generic* tool (analyze_document) into purpose-specific tools with their own contracts. The
docs consolidate closely related *actions* on one resource (create/review/merge a PR) into one tool with an `action` parameter. Both aim
at the same thing: every tool has one clear job the model can match.
howItWorks:
1. **List the jobs**, not the functions: what inputs arrive, what outputs are needed.
2. **One tool per distinct job** (split generic tools); **name it by purpose** (extract_web_results, not analyze_content).
3. **Describe** it: what it does, when to use it, when not to (name the neighbour), parameters and formats, what it returns and doesn't —
   3–4+ sentences. Add `input_examples` for format-sensitive or nested inputs.
4. **Read the system prompt** for keyword triggers (“whenever the user mentions…, use…”) and remove them.
5. **Test selection** with realistic, ambiguous requests — the lab's 11 test requests are a small version of that.
whereSeen:
- **Scenario 3 — Multi-Agent Research System** (Guide §5, p.4): web-results vs document tools (the analyze_content / analyze_document case).
- **Scenario 1 — Customer Support Resolution Agent** (Guide §5, p.3): get_customer / lookup_order boundaries and id formats.
- **Scenario 4 — Developer Productivity with Claude** (Guide §5, p.4): MCP tool descriptions vs built-in tools (see D2.3).

docsRefs.title: Define tools — tool definitions and best practices
How tool use works — the agentic loop
Handle tool calls — tool_result formatting, is_error

grounding.text: A tool definition has a name (must match ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$), a description, an input_schema (JSON Schema) and optionally input_examples (each must validate against the schema, else a 400).
grounding.ref: define-tools § Specifying client tools; Providing tool use examples

grounding.text: The API builds a special system prompt from your tool definitions, tool configuration and your own system prompt.

Extremely detailed descriptions are by far the most important factor in tool performance: say what the tool does, when to use it and when not, what each parameter means, and caveats/limitations such as what it does not return — at least 3–4 sentences, more for complex tools.
grounding.ref: define-tools § Best practices for tool definitions

grounding.text: Use input_examples for complex, nested or format-sensitive inputs (they cost ~20–50 tokens for simple examples, ~100–200 for complex ones); consolidate related operations into fewer tools (e.g. one tool with an action parameter); namespace tool names by service (github_list_prs, slack_send_message); return only high-signal information with stable identifiers.
grounding.ref: define-tools § Best practices; Providing tool use examples

grounding.text: Claude may add text before its tool_use blocks; code must not rely on that text's formatting.
Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism for tool selection; minimal descriptions make selection among similar tools unreliable.
Include input formats, example queries, edge cases and boundaries in tool descriptions.
Ambiguous or overlapping descriptions cause misrouting (e.g. analyze_content vs analyze_document with near-identical descriptions).
System-prompt wording affects selection: keyword-sensitive instructions can create unintended tool associations.

Skills: differentiate each tool's purpose, inputs, outputs and when to use it vs similar tools; rename tools and rewrite descriptions to remove overlap (analyze_content → extract_web_results); split generic tools into purpose-specific ones with defined input/output contracts (analyze_document → extract_data_points, summarize_content, verify_claim_against_source); review system prompts for keyword-sensitive instructions that override good descriptions.
The loop around tool calls (send → stop_reason tool_use → run → tool_result → repeat) is TS 1.1.

Guide vs docs on tool granularity: the guide splits a GENERIC tool into purpose-specific tools; the docs consolidate closely related ACTIONS (create/review/merge a PR) into one tool with an action parameter. Both aim at unambiguous selection with clear contracts — this page teaches both and when each applies.
grounding.ref: TS 2.1 S3 vs define-tools § Best practices

grounding.text: The simulated model's word-matching router (+1 per matching word, −2 for words in a “do not use” sentence, first tool wins a tie, system-prompt keyword rules override, ORD- formatting when the description says so) is invented to make the effect of descriptions visible and deterministic.

examPoints.text: Tool descriptions are the model's primary basis for choosing a tool; minimal descriptions make choosing between similar tools unreliable.
Descriptions should include input formats, example queries, edge cases and boundaries.
Ambiguous or overlapping descriptions cause misrouting (analyze_content vs analyze_document).
System-prompt wording influences tool choice: keyword-sensitive instructions create unintended associations.
Write descriptions that separate each tool's purpose, inputs, outputs and when to use it versus similar tools.
Rename tools and rewrite descriptions to remove overlap (analyze_content → extract_web_results).
Split generic tools into purpose-specific tools with defined input/output contracts (extract_data_points, summarize_content, verify_claim_against_source).
Review system prompts for keyword-sensitive instructions that override good descriptions.
The loop around the call: stop_reason tool_use → run the tool → return a tool_result → next iteration.

labIntro:
You write the **tool definitions and the system prompt**. A **simulated** model routes a small test set of realistic requests with them —
the lab prints, for every request, the tool it picked, the input it built and **why** (the words that matched, the “do not use” words that
counted against, or a tie). Four situations; all five mistakes are named in the exam guide (⭐).

labScenarios.title: Similar tools: web results vs documents
labScenarios.description: Two requests bring web search results, two bring uploaded/attached documents. Can your definitions tell them apart?

labScenarios.title: Three different jobs on documents
labScenarios.description: Extract exact values, summarise, and check a claim — each needs a different output.

labScenarios.title: A request that says “document” but brings web results
labScenarios.description: Does anything in your system prompt override the tool descriptions?

labScenarios.title: Input formats and boundaries
labScenarios.description: “order 1001” (the id format is ORD-####) and an order identified only by email.

variants.label: ✅ ⭐ Detailed, differentiated, purpose-specific, bounded
variants.code:
from utils.tool_select_lab import evaluate   # SIMULATED model that picks tools from their definitions

SYSTEM = "You are a research and support assistant. Choose the tool whose description matches the input you were given."

TOOLS = [
    {"name": "extract_web_results",
     "description": ("Extracts the key facts from web search results: the titles, snippets and URLs a web search returned. "
                     "Use it for any request whose input is web search results or web pages - including summarising them or "
                     "turning them into notes or a short write-up. "
                     "Returns a list of facts, each with the URL it came from. "
                     "Do not use it when the input is an uploaded, attached or PDF file, contract or report - use the file tools instead."),
     "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"results": {"type": "string", "description": "The raw web search results"}},
                      "required": ["results"]}},
    {"name": "extract_data_points",
     "description": ("Extracts specific data points - prices, dates, amounts, names, payment terms - from an uploaded or attached "
                     "document such as a PDF contract, invoice or report. Returns a list of {field, value, page}. "
                     "Use it when the user wants exact values pulled out of a document. "
                     "Do not use it for summaries, for checking claims, or for web search results."),
     "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"document_id": {"type": "string"}, "fields": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}}},
                      "required": ["document_id"]}},
    {"name": "summarize_content",
     "description": ("Writes a short summary or overview of an uploaded or attached document such as a report. "
                     "Use it when the user asks what a document says overall or wants it condensed. "
                     "Returns plain-text summary sentences. "
                     "Do not use it for web search results (use extract_web_results), to pull out exact values, or to verify a claim."),
     "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"document_id": {"type": "string"}, "max_sentences": {"type": "integer"}},
                      "required": ["document_id"]}},
    {"name": "verify_claim_against_source",
     "description": ("Checks whether a source document actually supports a specific claim and returns supported / contradicted / "
                     "not found with the evidence. Use it when the user asks whether a report or document supports, confirms or "
                     "backs up a claim. Do not use it for summaries or data extraction."),
     "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"claim": {"type": "string"}, "document_id": {"type": "string"}},
                      "required": ["claim", "document_id"]}},
    {"name": "lookup_order",
     "description": ("Looks up one order's status, amount and delivery date by its order id. "
                     "Order ids are in the form ORD-#### (for example ORD-1001); if the user gives only the number, prefix it "
                     "with ORD-. Returns status and amount, not customer details. "
                     "Do not use it when you only have an email address - use get_customer first."),
     "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"order_id": {"type": "string", "description": "Order id, e.g. ORD-1001"}},
                      "required": ["order_id"]}},
    {"name": "get_customer",
     "description": ("Finds a customer record by email address and returns the customer id and their recent order ids. "
                     "Use it when the user identifies an order or account by email. "
                     "It does not return order status."),
     "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"email": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["email"]}},
]

evaluate(TOOLS, SYSTEM)
variants.observe: Every test request is routed right — 4/4, 3/3, 2/2, 2/2 across the scenarios. Read the reasons in the output: the web request matches “web / search / result”, the PDF request matches “uploaded / pdf / contract”, and each “do not use … (use X)” sentence pushes a request away from the neighbouring tool. “order 1001” goes out as ORD-1001 because the description gives the format, and the email-only request goes to get_customer because lookup_order's description says when not to use it.
variants.why: Each description follows the docs' checklist — what the tool does, when to use it, when NOT to (naming the alternative), what it returns, what its input looks like — so near-neighbours are separable.

variants.fix: Write 3–4+ sentences per tool: what it does, when to use / not use it, parameters, what it returns and doesn't.

     "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"document_id": {"type": "string"}, "max_sentences": {"type": "integer"}},
                      "required": ["document_id"]}},
    {"name": "verify_claim_against_source",
     "description": ("Checks whether a source document actually supports a specific claim and returns supported / contradicted / "
                     "not found with the evidence. Use it when the user asks whether a report or document supports, confirms or "
                     "backs up a claim. Do not use it for summaries or data extraction."),
     "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"claim": {"type": "string"}, "document_id": {"type": "string"}},
                      "required": ["claim", "document_id"]}},
    {"name": "lookup_order",
     "description": "Looks up an order's status by order id. Returns status and amount.",   # WRONG: no format, no boundary
     "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"order_id": {"type": "string", "description": "The order id"}},
                      "required": ["order_id"]}},
    {"name": "get_customer",
     "description": "Finds a customer record and returns the customer id.",   # WRONG: no boundary
     "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"email": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["email"]}},
]

evaluate(TOOLS, SYSTEM)
variants.observe: lookup_order just “looks up an order's status by order id”: “order 1001” is sent as '1001', which the order system doesn't recognise, and “the order for alice@example.com” goes to lookup_order with no id at all: 0/2.
variants.why: Without the id format and the “only have an email → use get_customer” boundary, the model guesses both.
variants.fix: State formats with an example (ORD-1001), edge cases (bare numbers) and boundaries (what to use instead).

distractors.name: A · Minimal descriptions
distractors.looks: The name already says what it does.
distractors.fails: Similar tools can't be told apart; ties go to whatever is listed first.
distractors.instead: 3–4+ sentences: purpose, when to use/not use, params, returns.

distractors.name: B · Near-identical descriptions
distractors.fails: Detail that says the same thing gives no basis to choose.
distractors.instead: Rename by purpose; differentiate; add boundaries.

distractors.name: C · One generic tool
distractors.fails: No clear contract per job — extract, summarise and verify blur together.

distractors.name: D · Keyword rule in the system prompt
distractors.fails: It overrides good descriptions on any request with the word.
distractors.instead: Remove keyword triggers; review system prompts.

distractors.name: E · No formats or boundaries
distractors.looks: The model can figure out the format.
distractors.fails: Bare ids and email-only requests are guessed wrong.
distractors.instead: Formats with examples, edge cases, “use X instead”.

rows: What the model can match on
The same words for two tools

experiments: Run ✅ on similar_tools and read the matched words for each request.
Run ⭐❌ B and find the TIE lines. Then rename analyze_content and give it a web-only description — ties gone?
In ✅, delete the “Do not use it for web search results (use extract_web_results)” clause of summarize_content and run keyword_prompt.
In ✅, move get_customer above lookup_order and delete lookup_order's email boundary: which way does the tie fall now?
Add a line `SYSTEM += " Whenever the user mentions results, use verify_claim_against_source."` and run similar_tools.

questions.q: A research agent has two tools, analyze_content and analyze_document, both described as “Analyzes content and returns key information.” Logs from 1,000 requests show that about a third go to the wrong tool, and the misrouted calls are split roughly evenly between the two. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The model is too small to tell apart two tools with similar names, so it should be upgraded to a larger tier.
The descriptions are minimal and identical, so the model has nothing to tell the two tools apart with.
The system prompt lacks few-shot examples showing which of the two tools each kind of request should use.
The tools' input schemas share parameter names, so the model treats the two tools as interchangeable.
questions.explain: Tool descriptions are the main input the model uses to choose a tool. Two identical, minimal descriptions give it nothing to decide with, which is why the errors are split evenly. A blames the model for a design gap. C adds examples to work around the missing descriptions. D may add to the confusion, but it isn't the primary cause.

questions.q: In the same system, analyze_content is meant only for processing web search results, and analyze_document only for uploaded PDFs. The team has room for one change this sprint. Misrouting currently makes about 1 in 3 reports cite the wrong material. Which change best removes the misrouting?
opts: Merge both tools into one analyze tool that detects internally whether it received web results or a PDF.
Add a routing layer that inspects each input and calls the correct tool before the model sees the request.
Rename analyze_content to extract_web_results, and rewrite both descriptions to say what each takes and when.
Add five few-shot examples to the system prompt, showing which of the tools handles each type of input material.
questions.explain: Renaming and rewriting the descriptions removes the functional overlap at its source. It is low effort and high leverage. A is a bigger architectural change than the problem needs. B is an over-engineered layer that bypasses the model's own tool selection. D adds tokens while leaving the tools just as ambiguous.

questions.q: Customers say things like “order 1001”, but lookup_order accepts only IDs like ORD-1001. Its description is “Looks up an order.” Logs show that 28% of lookups fail on the ID format, and in another 9% of cases the agent calls get_customer instead. What is the best first fix?
opts: Add a PreToolUse hook that rewrites bare numbers into ORD- identifiers before lookup_order runs.
Add a line to the system prompt telling the agent to always prefix bare order numbers with ORD- before any lookup.
Merge lookup_order and get_customer into one lookup tool that accepts any identifier the customer gives.
Expand the description: the accepted ID format with examples, how to handle bare numbers, when not to use it.
questions.explain: A detailed description (input formats, examples, edge cases and boundaries against similar tools) fixes both the format failures and the wrong tool choice. A fixes the format but not the choice of get_customer. B addresses one symptom from outside the tool. C is a larger redesign than a first step needs.

questions.q: A single analyze_document tool is used to pull out figures, write summaries and check claims. Downstream code fails to parse about 15% of its outputs, because the shape of each result depends on which of the three jobs the model decided to do. What is the most robust redesign?
opts: Split it into purpose-specific tools (extract_data_points, summarize_content, verify_claim_against_source).
Keep the tool, and add a mode parameter that the downstream parser can read to guess the shape of each output.
Keep the tool, and tell the model in its description to always return JSON whichever job it performs.
Add a post-processing step that uses a second model call to convert each output into the expected shape.
questions.explain: Splitting a generic tool into purpose-specific tools gives each one a defined input/output contract, and makes the model's choice explicit. B still leaves one tool with shifting outputs, now with a guess added. C gives consistent syntax but no consistent shape. D adds another model call that can fail in the same way.

questions.q: After the team carefully rewrote every tool description, misrouting fell from 30% to 8%. The remaining errors share a pattern: any request that mentions a “report”, such as “summarise this report”, goes to generate_report. Both tools' descriptions are accurate. What should the team check next?
opts: The model's temperature setting, which may be making tool choice random on requests that mention reports.
The order of the tools in the request, since the model may favour whichever tool is listed first.
The system prompt, for keyword-driven instructions such as “if the user mentions a report, use generate_report”.
The generate_report input schema, which may accept so many different input types that the model never rules the tool out.
questions.explain: An error that follows a keyword points to a keyword-sensitive instruction in the system prompt, which can override good descriptions. A would give random errors, not a consistent pattern. B: nothing in the errors points to position. They follow a word. D doesn't explain why the word “report” triggers it.

questions.q: To save tokens, a platform team caps every tool description at one short line across 12 developer-productivity agents. Within a week, wrong-tool calls rise from 4% to 15%. The team asks whether to add few-shot routing examples to compensate. What does the tool-use documentation suggest?
opts: Add the few-shot examples, since they are the documented primary lever for tool-selection accuracy.
Restore detailed descriptions, the most important factor: several sentences on what, when and caveats.
Keep the one-line descriptions, and move the lost detail into each tool's parameter names instead.
Cut each agent to three tools, since short descriptions work well enough when there are only a few tools.
questions.explain: The docs call detailed descriptions the most important factor in tool performance, and suggest several sentences covering what the tool does, when to use it and its caveats. A treats examples as the primary lever, which descriptions are. C squeezes documentation into parameter names. D cuts functionality to fit a token-saving rule.

faq.q: Does the model really just match words?
faq.a: No — the lab's router is a deliberately simple stand-in so you can see why a choice was made. The documented point is that the description is what Claude uses to decide, so it must carry the purpose, boundaries and formats.
Split a tool that does unrelated jobs with different outputs; consolidate closely related actions on the same resource behind one `action` parameter. Either way, one clear job per tool.
Optional example inputs on a tool definition (each must validate against the schema, else a 400). Useful for nested or format-sensitive inputs; they cost roughly 20–50 tokens each for simple ones.
tool_choice controls WHETHER and WHICH tool must be called (auto / any / tool / none) — that's D2.2. This page is about making the model's own choice right.
